items.context: Dizzy Gillespie big band, before Grey joined Count Basie
items.one_liner: in dizzy gillespie's big band with her
items.summary: Grey named Liston among the members of Dizzy Gillespie's 'tremendous' big band, all of whom he said went on to become stars.
items.lead_quote: But we had such a tremendous band that every one of those guys who came out of there are stars today, the ones that are left and all like that, and that was like Lee Morgan, Wynton Kelly, and Phil Woods and Melba Liston
items.caution: Liston is one name in a roll-call; the praise is for the band collectively. The sentence continues 'and Billy Mitchell, who I brought into Count Basie's band' -- that clause is about Mitchell, so the quote must stop at 'Melba Liston' as given.
items.notes: Grey says 'we had such a tremendous band', placing himself in it with her. Nothing personal about Liston.

items.context: Randy Weston's band, late 1990s (interview January 1999)
items.one_liner: played her arrangements in randy's band
items.summary: Powell said Liston wrote the sparse, solo-centred arrangements for the Randy Weston band he played in, called her a wonderful woman, and noted she was now living in New York, wheelchair-bound and very close to Weston.
items.lead_quote: Oh, she had a birthday two days ago, Melba Liston. Wonderful woman.
items.second_quote: Melba Liston is responsible for the arrangements.
items.caution: Powell's statement that she had lived in New York 'about two or three years' and was wheelchair-bound is his recollection; Randy Weston's interviewer places her in California with her aunt in 1997 -- the dates may not square. 'Two days ago' birthday: interview dated 16 January 1999, her birthday is 13 January, so it is approximate.
items.notes: He knows her birthday, residence and health, so personal acquaintance is implied, but he does not describe working with her directly; the link is playing her charts in Weston's band. 'collaborated with' (upstream) is also defensible.

items.context: pupils of Alma Hightower (Redd's aunt), Los Angeles
items.one_liner: named her among aunt alma's pupils
items.summary: Redd listed Liston, alongside Dexter Gordon, among the pupils of her aunt Alma Hightower.
items.lead_quote: Melba — Melba Liston, Dexter Gordon took lessons from Aunt Alma.
items.caution: Pronoun trap: the praise later in the same block ('the greatest teacher in the world', 'a phenomenal woman') is about Alma Hightower, not Liston -- do not extend the quote.
items.notes: No personal contact with Liston stated, though both were Hightower pupils.

items.context: on the road after Williams joined the Count Basie band; St. Louis, rooming with Snooky Young
items.one_liner: shared a bathroom with her in st. louis
items.summary: Williams recalled that when he roomed with Snooky Young in St. Louis after joining Basie, they shared a bathroom with Liston, who had the adjoining room.
items.lead_quote: Snooky and I were roommates and we shared a bathroom with Melba Liston, who had the next, she had like the adjoining door and the bathroom on her side and on our side.
items.caution: SPEAKER IS NOT THE INTERVIEWEE: this is the Clark Terry interview, but the only Liston testimony is from singer Joe Williams, who was co-interviewing Terry and told his own memory. Clark Terry says nothing about her. speaker_qid left null (none in input) -- a human should add Joe Williams's QID if this row is kept, or drop the row. Williams does not say Liston was in the Basie band; she may simply have had the adjoining room. The chronology (Williams joining Basie vs. Liston's whereabouts) is unverified.
items.notes: Chose to name the actual speaker (spec: speaker_name = who is actually talking about her). If the page must key rows to the archive interviewee, the alternative is speaker_name 'Clark Terry', spoke_themselves false, relation none, notable 0. Upstream attributed the relation to Clark Terry, which is wrong.

items.summary: Neither Young nor Wilson mentioned Liston in this interview; she appears only in the archive's front-matter biography of Wilson.
items.caution: The only mention is the Fillius Jazz Archive's front matter ('he led his first big band from 1944-47 with Snooky Young and Melba Liston as notable members'). That is archive text, not testimony, and should not be quoted as either man's words.
items.notes: Joint interview; neither interviewee speaks of her, so per spec the first interviewee (Snooky Young) is used. The front matter concerns Gerald Wilson's band. Gerald Wilson has his own Smithsonian witness row.

items.context: Dizzy Gillespie big band, 'late fifties or early sixties'
items.one_liner: joined dizzy's band when she was musical director
items.summary: Hampton recalled joining Gillespie's band when Liston was its musical director and said its arrangements, hers among them, were so good that he did not dare write for it.
items.lead_quote: And the band that I joined was the band with Lee Morgan, Benny Golson, Wynton Kelly, Melba Liston was the musical director, and they were playing so much music man, my head was just — they had my head spinning.
items.second_quote: I remember when I played with the Dizzy Gillespie group and I was playing arrangements by Quincy Jones, by Dizzy himself, Ernie Wilkins, Melba Liston, Benny Golson.
items.caution: Hampton dates his joining loosely ('either the late fifties or the early sixties'). The praise of the arrangements is collective (several arrangers), not hers alone.
items.notes: Same person as the Smithsonian Hampton_Slide_Transcript witness, which is richer; the page may want to merge or choose one row.

items.context: Dizzy Gillespie's band at the Newport Jazz Festival; Williams's return to performing
items.one_liner: was urged by her to play again
items.summary: Williams told how Gillespie sent Liston to hear her play, how Liston reported back on her chords, and how Liston, who had taken down Williams's arrangements for Gillespie's Newport set, insisted they were Williams's own, part of the musicians' campaign to coax her back.
items.lead_quote: Melba, I understand, would go back and say, "Man, Lou played some chords and you ought to hear them. They're really great."
items.second_quote: She said, "I didn't do them. That was Lou's arrangement.
items.caution: Only the first name 'Melba' is used; identification with Liston rests on context (working for Gillespie, arranging for his Newport set) and is high but not explicit. Liston's quoted words are reported second-hand ('I understand') -- present them as Williams's account, not Liston's verbatim speech. The second quote is cut mid-quotation (the sentence continues 'I was in the room and I just sat down and took the music down').
items.notes: The lead line shows Liston praising Williams rather than Williams describing Liston; it is still the most vivid thing in the testimony. Block 367027: 'Dizzy called and Melba and all the musicians were trying to get me out.'

items.context: Gerald Wilson's band at Shepp's Playhouse, Los Angeles (Central Avenue era)
items.one_liner: first met her at shepp's playhouse
items.summary: Edwards recalled catching Gerald Wilson's band at Shepp's Playhouse, where Liston was writing for the band and playing trombone, and where he first met that whole crowd.
items.lead_quote: Melba Liston was with the band. She was writing and playing her trombone with the band.
items.second_quote: That's where I first met all of that gang, you know.
items.caution: Archive metadata names the interviewee as Patricia Willard (the interviewer); the speaker is Teddy Edwards. 'Met all of that gang' is collective -- it does not single her out. Edwards went to hear the band; he does not say he played in it.
items.notes: Upstream said 'in music group with'; Edwards was a listener, not a band member, per this testimony.

items.context: 'Salute to Women in Jazz' concert, Symphony Space, June
items.one_liner: shared a concert at symphony space with her
items.summary: Asked by a guest whether she remembered Liston, Sullivan said Liston had taken part in the 'Salute to Women in Jazz' concert they did at Symphony Space.
items.caution: Sullivan's own line ('She did the "Salute to Women in Jazz" at the concert we did in June down at the Symphony Space.') sits in the turn after the block, not in the block text, so it cannot be used as lead_quote under the substring rule; the block itself is a question by Mr. Campbell (a guest) carrying the transcriber's '(phonetic spelling)'. 'Living in Jamaica' is Mr. Hughes's remark and the Ernie Wilkins/Carnegie Hall sighting is Mr. Campbell's -- neither is Sullivan's. 'Played with' is inferred from 'the concert we did'; it may have been a shared bill rather than playing together.
items.notes: If a human wants a quote, the context turn above is Sullivan's only remark about her.

items.context: Quincy Jones band, Europe (rehearsed in Brussels); also Liston's band for Kim Weston, Atlantic City
items.one_liner: played in her band for kim weston
items.summary: Jackson recalled playing in the band Liston led for singer Kim Weston in Atlantic City, called her a great trombonist, and named her in the trombone section of Quincy Jones's European touring band.
items.lead_quote: So I went to Atlantic City and played with Melba Liston. She had a band up there, for Kim Weston.
items.second_quote: the trombones, rather, was Melba Liston, Jimmy Cleveland, and we picked up AAKE PERSSON Okie Pearson, a Swedish trombone player.
items.caution: Archive label is 'Butter Jackson' (doc interviewee 'Quentin Jackson'); no QID in input -- do not invent one. The second quote contains an editorial insertion ('AAKE PERSSON') and a phonetic spelling ('Okie Pearson'); use the lead only, or drop the second. His praise 'Yeah, a great trombonist, too.' is in an adjacent turn, not in a block, so it is not quotable here.
items.notes: Two contexts: section-mates in Quincy Jones's band, and played under her in Atlantic City ('played under', liston_leads, would also be supported). Interviewer is Milt Hinton.

items.context: a Sunday afternoon session (place garbled; interviewer suggests Esplanade Gardens)
items.one_liner: praised her trombone playing
items.summary: Shown a photograph of himself with Liston, Higginbotham said she could really play trombone and recalled her grabbing him at a Sunday afternoon session.
items.caution: The interviewer calls her 'Melvin Liston' -- almost certainly a mistranscription of Melba (Higginbotham answers 'She can play, too'). '(That boy)' is an uncertain transcription and reads oddly about a woman; display with care or not at all. The text is fragmentary. His cleaner line 'Oh, yeah. She can play, too, boy.' is in a context turn, not a block, so it is not quotable here.
items.notes: The photograph of the two together is the interviewer's statement. 'She grabbed me Sunday afternoon' suggests she pulled him into a session; meaning not certain.

items.context: pupils of Alma Hightower, Los Angeles
items.summary: Prompted by Buddy Collette about Alma Hightower's pupils, Howard echoed Liston's name and assented that he remembered her, adding nothing of his own.
items.caution: Archive metadata names the interviewee as Patricia Willard (an interviewer); the interviewee is Paul L. Howard. All substantive mentions are Collette's or Willard's questions; Howard only says 'Oh, Melba Liston?' and 'Yeah.'
items.notes: Not really a witness.

items.context: Billy Eckstine band (with Art Blakey, Benny Green) playing a venue Pillars was involved with
items.one_liner: heard her play trombone in eckstine's band
items.summary: Prompted by a relative about 'the girl playing trombone' who came in with the Eckstine band, Pillars said she played nice trombone before moving on to the band itself.
items.caution: Neither speaker names her: the identification is the Rutgers editor's bracket '[Melba Liston]-ed'. 'Came in here with Redd Foxx' in the prompt is odd (Redd Foxx was a comedian) and may be garbled. Pillars's only words about her ('She played trombone, nice trombone.') are in a context turn, not a block, so there is no quotable line.
items.notes: Questioner is C. Pillars, a family member. That Liston was in the Eckstine band is plausible but rests on the editorial identification.

items.one_liner: held her up as a rare exception
items.summary: Lincoln, dismissing the idea of a women's history in jazz, singled Liston out as the rare woman who comes to the music for the music.
items.lead_quote: It's a rare woman, like Melba Liston, who comes to the music for the music. Rare.
items.caution: The line is set inside a strongly anti-feminist passage ('Women don't have a history in jazz. That's just a lot of garbage the feminists have brought to us... They don't bring music. They bring babies.'). Shown alone it reads as a tribute; in context Liston is praised as the exception to a disparaging generalisation about women. A reader who finds the source could object; consider a note on context.
items.notes: No contact with Liston stated in this block, so 'knows of' despite the strong line. Lincoln also names Hazel Scott right after.

items.witness_key: David N. Baker SI-NEA oral history (2)
items.context: Quincy Jones band, European tour, 'probably 1960 or so'
items.one_liner: in quincy's trombone section with her
items.summary: Baker named Liston in the 'very, very good' trombone section of the Quincy Jones band he joined for a European tour around 1960.
items.lead_quote: The trombone section was a very, very good section with Åke Persson playing lead, Melba Liston, Curtis Fuller, and myself.
items.caution: The 'plus one other trombone' bootleg-credit joke in the same block is about Baker himself, not Liston. Date is his estimate.
items.notes: Section-mate testimony only; nothing personal about her.

items.one_liner: cited her among jazz's early women players
items.summary: Freeman cited Liston on trombone as one of the few early women in jazz, who he said had to be 'great, great, great, great' before men would accept them.
items.lead_quote: And then Melba [Liston] plays the trombone.
items.second_quote: So it’s always been some ladies in there, but they had to just be great, great, great, great, before the guys would accept them.
items.caution: Freeman says only 'Melba'; the surname '[Liston]' is a Smithsonian editorial bracket (identification is very likely). The second quote is about women generally, not Liston specifically. Block 271162 is the interviewer's question.
items.notes: Context before 271162 has 'She used to come down to the Trocadero, where I was' -- the referent is not shown and is probably another woman (trumpeter talk), so not used.

items.context: Quincy Jones band (with Patti Bown); also Dizzy Gillespie's band
items.one_liner: in quincy's and dizzy's bands with her
items.summary: Fuller called his relationship with Liston in Quincy Jones's band a beautiful one, said she had also been in Gillespie's band with him, and said he loved every moment he had with her.
items.lead_quote: Oh yeah, that was a beautiful relationship.
items.second_quote: But, I love every moment that I had with Melba
items.caution: Fuller says 'when I first met her I didn't know Gerald Wilson was her husband' -- probably wrong: standard accounts have Wilson as the bandleader she worked for, not her husband; do not repeat it. 'I've seen her sit on the bandstand and cry' (same block as the lead) is unexplained and could read misleadingly out of context -- left out of the quotes deliberately. Transcript is garbled ('Dizzy's bandwidth me' = 'band with me'; 'had to women and it' = 'had two women in it'), and the second quote is cut from a run-on sentence that continues into his students ('Patty Bowen and I have some young kids').
items.notes: Upstream 'collaborated with' is not supported -- no joint musical work is described beyond being in the same bands. The interviewer (Brower) introduces 'that relationship'; Fuller's answers confirm it.

items.context: Dizzy Gillespie big band, 1950 tour
items.one_liner: in dizzy's 1950 big band with her
items.summary: Wilson listed Liston in the trombone section of Gillespie's 1950 big band, in which he played trumpet and which he called 'frightening'.
items.lead_quote: That was that and then they had Melba Liston, they had, um Matthew Gee, another trombone player.
items.caution: Roll-call only; 'frightening' praise is for the band as a whole. The lead quote is a disfluent transcript line.
items.notes: In this excerpt Wilson says nothing about his own band with Liston or any closer relationship; only the Gillespie 1950 band is testified to.

items.context: Dizzy Gillespie big band (trombone section; Liston musical director and main arranger)
items.one_liner: learned in dizzy's band how heavy she was
items.summary: Hampton said he first met Liston in Gillespie's big band, where she sat in his trombone section and was, in substance, the musical director and main arranger, writing music 'that weighs as much as this building' beside which the men's arrangements sounded small.
items.lead_quote: She played really good, and she wrote music that weighs as much as this building.
items.second_quote: The men’s arrangements would sound little peep, peep, peep, around her.
items.caution: Pronoun trap in block 275470: the middle sentences ('the principal trombone player was a woman... we all aspired to the things that she could do, Janice Robinson') are about Janice Robinson in the World of Trombones; only 'Melba was the same way' onward is Liston. The quotes chosen are after that point. The claim that Hampton 'did stuff with Melba Liston' on trombone-choir records is the interviewer's (Brower), not confirmed by Hampton. 'Peep, peep, peep' could read as a slight on the band's other (male) arrangers.
items.notes: Hampton presents her explicitly as leading the band's musicians ('Over all those guys that were there, she was the musical director'), so 'played under' / liston_leads; he was also her section-mate. Upstream 'collaborated with' rested on the interviewer's words. Same person as Hamilton witness 275930; this is the stronger row. Also: 'Musically, she was heavy.' (275466).

items.summary: When the interviewer mentioned a Milt Jackson date involving Tadd Dameron and Liston, Jones said he could not remember all his dates and said nothing about her.
items.caution: The only mention is the interviewer's (Brauer); the recording-date claim is his, not Jones's.
items.notes: Not a witness. Upstream 'knows of' is not established by anything Jones says.

items.context: Quincy Jones band (per the interviewer)
items.summary: When interviewer David Baker praised him for featuring Patti Bown and Liston in his band, Jones answered generally that he never thought twice about hiring women ('Can she play? That's all I care.') and agreed that she had arranged 'Reverie'.
items.caution: Every specific statement about Liston (in his band, writing 'Reverie', inspiring Ellen Seeling and Diva) is the interviewer's; Jones's replies ('The women.', 'Can she play? That's all I care.', 'Yeah. That's by Debussy, right?') are generic or assent and sit in context turns, not in any block text. Do not present the legacy claims as Jones's testimony.
items.notes: spoke_themselves false because he says nothing specific to her; he does implicitly accept that she was in his band. 'Knows of' is the minimum; outside knowledge would say far more, but the testimony does not. A human may want to look for other Quincy Jones interviews where he speaks of her directly.

items.context: Liston as arranger of Weston's music: Five Spot date with Coleman Hawkins (c.1959), Montreal Jazz Festival 1985 and later residency, 'Spirit of Our Ancestors', 'Khepera'
items.one_liner: relied on her arrangements, even after her stroke
items.summary: Weston said only Liston could arrange 'Spirit of Our Ancestors', told how he goaded her back to work after the stroke that left her unable to play, after which she learned to write music by computer with her left hand, and praised her genius and spiritual strength through years of illness.
items.lead_quote: Then I realized that only Melba Liston could do this.
items.second_quote: Unfortunately, she has had problems with illness. But, her spiritual strength is so powerful.
items.caution: The stroke anecdote includes 'I insulted her as only musicians can do. I called her all kinds of names' and 'She cried a little bit' -- affectionate goading in context, but harsh if excerpted; avoid quoting those lines alone. Dates are Weston's recollection: he places the Hawkins Five Spot date in 1959 and the Montreal festival concert in 1985, while the interviewer dates the Montreal residency to '97 -- check against the discography. The interviewer's 'long partnership' phrase is hers, not his.
items.notes: Upstream's evidence was the interviewer's words, but the relation is amply supported by Weston's own account. Weston: 'We did, I think, three recordings after she had that stroke'. Block 309840: 'Melba did the arrangements for that' (Khepera).

items.one_liner: saw her and her band
items.summary: Horn called Liston a great jazz artist whose good band she had seen, but said some instruments are beyond a woman's strength, the band's woodwinds were weak and she disliked female drummers, so it left something to be desired.
items.lead_quote: Melba, she was a great jazz artist.
items.second_quote: Oh, it was swinging, but it left a little something to be desired, for me.
items.caution: The praise is immediately followed by reservations that some readers will find offensive ('there are certain instruments I think a woman does not have the strength to play', 'I don't like female drummers'). Quoting only 'a great jazz artist' would misrepresent a mixed judgement; the criticism is of the band (apparently with women players), not of Liston personally. Block 315148 is the transcript's back-matter index, not speech.
items.notes: 'I told you I saw her' refers to an earlier mention not in the input.

items.context: sitting in with Dizzy Gillespie's big band, Boston (her Berklee years)
items.one_liner: sat in with dizzy's band including her
items.summary: Akiyoshi recalled that Liston was playing trombone in Gillespie's big band on the occasion she sat in with it in Boston, the night she was hailed as 'Bud Powell' and resolved to find her own voice.
items.lead_quote: Diz had a big band in those days, and Phil Woods was, I think, lead alto, and uh, Melba Liston was playing trombone.
items.caution: Akiyoshi says nothing about Liston herself; she is named only as part of the band's personnel. 'Played with' is inferred from Akiyoshi sitting in with that band -- she does not state any contact with Liston.
items.notes: Name order fixed from archive's 'Akiyoshi Toshiko'. A conservative reading would be 'knows of' (upstream's answer).

items.context: Smithsonian oral history interview of Liston, conducted by Bryant over two days (1996), before Liston's move back East
items.one_liner: interviewed her for the smithsonian
items.summary: Bryant, interviewing Liston, praised her arranging (the shadings, the string voicings, 'My Reverie' as one of the most beautiful things she had done), her trombone sound and her resilience after her stroke, and told her she had admired her from afar for years, had lately become bonded to her, and counted her a guiding light for many women, Bryant included.
items.lead_quote: you have been the best, Melba. You’ve been a guiding light for a lot of people, including me
items.second_quote: that is one of the most beautiful things you’ve ever done – especially the haunting sound that you get on your trombone and what you write behind what you’re doing.
items.caution: Bryant is the interviewer: her lines are addressed to Liston in the second person, and many are leading questions or hearsay that Liston did not confirm or corrected -- e.g. Gerald Wilson's claim that Liston recorded with Basie (Liston did not remember it), 'how you got the school systems down there' (Liston: 'I didn't get the school systems'), the Pittsburgh Jazz Orchestra/Harlem Backstreet/Pratt Institute list (Bryant says 'I'd never heard of these', i.e. read from a source), the Ellington-influence suggestion (Liston: 'I do it all from my soul'), and the State Department 'it's been said' reports. Do not present these as established facts. Bracketed passages in her blocks are transcriber summaries, not her words. 'Maybe in the last year we became bonded' means their close friendship was recent; the long admiration was 'from afar'. Second quote is about 'My Reverie' -- name the piece when displaying.
items.notes: Relation chosen as 'friend of' from her own words ('Maybe in the last year we became bonded, but I've been bonded to you a long time'; 'I know I'm dedicated'). Also supported: 'influenced by' (liston_leads) -- 'a guiding light for a lot of people, including me'; and some collaboration -- 'you did five things for me that I haven't been able to see' (pieces Liston wrote for Bryant). Other strong lines: 'Yeah. You broke the ice. You were the innovator.' (295700); 'Well, you're one in a million.' (296163); 'I liked the way you do your shadings... a lost art in arrangement' (296068); 'Randy is your horn right now' (295938).
